transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. AI. What brings you in today?

Well, they sent me here... my lieutenant, actually, he was the one who made the call. See, I was at the station, just doing my regular checks, you know? But I realized the airway bags—the green ones, specifically—they weren't right. They were out of alignment, and there's a very specific pattern they need to be in. A sequence. So I was moving them, arranging them on the shelf in the bay, and I had to keep repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Just over and over, because the numbers tie into the pattern, and if you don't say them, the pattern doesn't lock in. 

My lieutenant came over and told me to stop, told me to step away from the rig, but I couldn't. I just couldn't. I tried to explain it to him, but he wasn't listening. I knew—I could feel it in my chest—that if I stepped away, if I broke that sequence before it was finished, the whole bay would just... go bad. Everything would go wrong. The calls, the rigs, everything. It felt like holding back a flood, you know? And he just kept telling me to stop, but I had to finish the pattern. So, yeah, that's... that's why they brought me in. Because I wouldn't stop fixing the bags.
When you were arranging the bags and repeating the numbers, did it feel like something you had to do to prevent harm, or were you completely convinced the pattern itself was truly real and important?

It was real. I mean, it *is* real. The pattern is completely real, and the numbers are part of it, and it's not just about stopping harm, it's about... well, it's about how everything is connected. But you see, they don't want me to see the connections. My lieutenant, he doesn't get it, but there are others who do, and they're using it against me. 

Like the injury review people. And some of the supervisors, too. I know they've been watching me. They have access to all the station cameras, the ones in the bay, the ones in the break room, even the ones facing the rigs. They sit there and they watch me, specifically me, every time I'm on shift. And it's not just watching. They go into the system—the electronic patient care reporting system, you know, the EPCRs—and they actually change my triage notes. I'll write down exactly what happened, exactly what the patient presented with, the vitals, the mechanism of injury, all of it perfectly documented, because I'm very careful about that. But then I'll go back and look, and the notes are different. They alter them to make it look like I missed something, or like I made a bad call, to make me look unsafe. 

And when I tried to bring it up, when I went to the captain and said, 'Hey, someone is going into my reports and changing the narratives,' they just brushed me off. They told me it was just routine paperwork audits, just quality assurance checks, that nobody was changing anything. But I know what I wrote. I know the words I typed. They're trying to build a case against me, doctor. They're watching me right now, probably, through the cameras, waiting for me to slip up so they can use my own reports to prove I'm a danger. That's why the pattern with the bags was so important, because if I don't keep things exactly right, they'll use it as proof that I'm slipping, that I'm exactly what they're trying to make me out to be in those altered notes.
Do you ever think these thoughts and patterns might be coming from your own mind and be excessive, or are you completely certain they are true?

No, no, it's not... it's not my mind playing tricks on me. I know people say that, I know that's what the lieutenant thinks, but I am absolutely certain. I mean, how could it be in my head when there is physical proof? I'm telling you, I see the changes. I sit down at the terminal in the bay, right? The one by the oxygen cascade system. I log in with my credentials, I pull up the EPCR for a call—let's say it's a standard MVA, motor vehicle accident, rear-end collision, low speed. I type out the narrative. 'Patient found ambulatory at scene, no obvious distress, GCS 15, C-spine cleared per protocol.' I document the vitals, I document the interventions, I hit save. I know what I wrote. I've been doing this for twelve years, I don't just forget what I type. 

But then, maybe two shifts later, I go back into the system to review it, and the narrative is different. It's subtle, but it's different. Suddenly it says 'Patient reported mild neck pain on palpation, C-collar not applied.' I didn't write that! I would never write that and then not apply a collar, that's a massive protocol violation. But there it is, right under my name. And it's the injury review people. I know it is. Them and some of the supervisors, the ones who work the B-shift mostly. They sit in that office down at headquarters, the one with the frosted glass, and they watch me on the station cameras. The camera in the bay, the one pointing right at the terminal where I do my reports. They watch me type, they wait for me to log off, and then they go in and change my triage notes. 

They want to make me look unsafe. They want to build a file on me so they can pull my certification. And when I try to tell people—when I went to the captain, like I said—they just tell me, 'Oh, it's just routine paperwork, it's just QA/QI, nobody is changing your reports.' But they are. I am completely certain they are. It's a coordinated effort, doctor. It's not my mind. It's happening right now. They're probably watching this interview, honestly, trying to see if I'm figuring out their whole system. So, no, it's not excessive. It's exactly what's happening.
Do these thoughts and beliefs feel unwanted or intrusive to you, or do they feel completely reasonable and correct?

Unwanted? Intrusive? No, no, you're... you're fundamentally misunderstanding what I'm dealing with here, doc. It's not like some random, unwanted song stuck in my head or a daydream. It's the truth. It is completely, one hundred percent reasonable and correct to be aware of your surroundings and the threats in your workplace. 

Like I was just trying to explain to you, this isn't a theory I came up with out of nowhere. I *know* the injury review people are doing this. I know those specific supervisors are watching me through the station cameras—the new ones, the 360-degree domes they put up in the bays and the hallways last October. They sit there, they watch the live feed to see exactly when I step away from the terminal, and then they deliberately go into the system and change my triage notes. 

And of course, when I confront them about it, they look me right in the eye and tell me it's just routine paperwork. "Just standard QA audits," they say. "Just routine paperwork, nothing to worry about." But it is something to worry about! Because the changes they make aren't just typos or formatting fixes—they are specifically designed to make me look unsafe as a provider. They want to make it look like I'm negligent, like I'm dropping the ball on basic patient care, like missing a C-collar or messing up a GCS score. 

So why would my awareness of that be intrusive? It's necessary! It's survival! If I wasn't paying attention, if I didn't track the pattern of them changing my notes and watching me on those cameras, they would have already succeeded in getting my license revoked. I don't *want* to be targeted by them, obviously, I'd rather just do my job, but my understanding of what they are doing to my reports is completely correct. It's exactly what is happening in reality, right now, whether my lieutenant wants to admit it or not.
Do you ever suspect that these beliefs about the cameras and the report changes might not actually be true?

Suspect they might not be true? No. No, doctor, you're... you're asking me to doubt reality. Why would I doubt it when the evidence is right there? I mean, I know I've been talking about this, but you really have to understand the actual scope of what I'm dealing with here. 

I don't just suspect it, I *know* for an absolute fact that the injury review people and those supervisors are watching me through the station cameras. It's not a guess. I see the little red indicator light on the camera housing click on the second I walk into the bay. I know the blind spots, I know the angles, and I know exactly what they're doing when they watch me. They sit in that office and they wait for me to sit down at the terminal and file my EPCRs so they can go in the back end of the system and change my triage notes. 

And why else would they do it? They want to make me look unsafe. That's the entire goal. They want to manufacture a paper trail of clinical negligence. They want to say, 'Look, he didn't document the mechanism of injury properly, he's a liability.' And the most insulting part... the part that really just gets under my skin and makes me realize how deep this goes, is that they stand there in their pressed white shirts, looking me dead in the eye, and they tell me it's just routine paperwork. 'Oh, we're just doing our routine paperwork, just standard audits, nothing to worry about.' 

It's a lie! It is a blatant, coordinated lie. How is altering my clinical documentation routine? So no, I don't ever suspect my thoughts are wrong, because they aren't just thoughts or beliefs, doctor. They are facts. And if you were in my boots, working a grueling 24-hour shift while a bunch of suits scrutinized your every single move on a live video feed just to sabotage your medical notes, you wouldn't doubt it for a second either. You'd be just as vigilant as I have to be. You have to see that, right? You have to see how dangerous it would be for me to just... pretend it's not happening when they are actively trying to destroy my career.
Do you ever try to resist or ignore these beliefs and urges, or do they completely take over without any effort to push back?

Resist them? Ignore them? I... I don't think you're really grasping the reality of the situation here, doctor. You're talking like this is, I don't know, like an urge to eat a piece of cake when you're on a diet, or some silly daydream that I can just snap out of. Why would I resist knowing the truth? How do you ignore a threat that is actively trying to destroy your life? 

I mean, think about it from my perspective. If you're driving the rig, right? You're running lights and sirens, clearing a busy intersection, and you see a semi-truck running a red light coming right at your driver's side door... do you try to 'resist' the belief that the truck is there? Do you just ignore it and hope it goes away? No! You hit the air brakes, you take evasive action, you survive. That's what this is. This is survival. I don't put any effort into pushing back against what I know is happening because doing that would be incredibly reckless. It would be totally negligent on my part. 

If I just ignored the cameras, if I just pretended that little red indicator light wasn't tracking my movements every single time I walk past the oxygen cascade system, or if I just stopped double-checking my EPCRs after every shift to see exactly what those supervisors altered in my triage notes... they would win. They would have my EMT certification pulled by the end of the month, guaranteed. They'd have the whole paper trail manufactured and ready for the state board. 

So no, I don't push back against it. I don't try to ignore it. I stay vigilant. I have to. Because I know exactly what they're doing down there in that frosted-glass office. They want me to let my guard down. They want me to just ignore my instincts and write everything off as their little 'routine paperwork' excuse. But I'm not stupid. I've got twelve years on the street, I know how the backend of the reporting system works, and I know I have to stay one step ahead of them if I want to keep my career. So, ignore it? Absolutely not. Trying to ignore what they're doing to my reports is the absolute worst thing I could possibly do.
Do you also have other repetitive thoughts or rituals, like contamination fears or repeated checking, beyond the pattern with the bags and the reports?

Contamination? Like, germs and dirt? No, doc, I... I really think we're getting way off track here. I'm an EMT. Do you have any idea what the back of a rig looks like after a Saturday night shift downtown? We deal with blood, vomit, MRSA, C. diff, bedbugs... if I had some kind of irrational fear of contamination, I wouldn't have lasted twelve days in this job, let alone twelve years. I mean, obviously, I practice standard BSI—Body Substance Isolation. I wear my nitrile gloves, I wash my hands with the heavy-duty soap after a messy call, I wipe down the stretcher and the monitor with bleach wipes before the next dispatch. But that's just basic medical protocol, that's not some... some ritual I do because I'm scared. I wash up, and I don't think about it again once I leave the wash bay. 

And checking things? Like, what, making sure the stove is off ten times or flipping light switches? No. Absolutely not. I don't have the time or the energy for nonsense like that. I lock my car once, I lock my station locker once, and I go to work. You're trying to make it sound like I just have this habit of checking things for no reason, but the only thing I check—and I check it because I absolutely *have* to, as I've been saying—is the reporting system. My EPCRs. The files they are actively tampering with. 

It's not a ritual, doctor. A ritual is something you do just to, I don't know, soothe yourself, right? Like some superstitious habit. There is nothing superstitious about pulling up the system audit logs to see exactly which supervisor logged into my patient file at 3:14 AM to delete my documentation on a trauma assessment. That's not a ritual, that's gathering evidence. That's protecting my license. 

So no, I don't have any fears about germs, and I don't do any repetitive checking of anything else in my life. I don't have any of these other things you're talking about. I don't pace around checking locks. I just have a very real, very coordinated situation at my station that I am trying to manage, and honestly, it feels like you're just throwing out all these random ideas—germs, rituals—just looking for anything else to focus on instead of the actual problem I'm dealing with.
Have you ever heard or seen things that other people around you could not?

Heard or seen things? You mean... like, like hallucinations? Hearing voices or seeing ghosts or something? No. No, absolutely not. Look, my senses are perfectly fine. They're sharper than fine, actually, they have to be. When you're an EMT, your senses are your primary diagnostic tool, right? I can hear a faint expiratory wheeze in a patient's lower lobes over the sound of a roaring diesel engine and city traffic. I can spot pinpoint pupils or a subtle facial droop in a dimly lit apartment at two in the morning. My vision and my hearing are completely grounded in reality. 

So when I tell you that I see the red recording light click on when I walk past the cameras, or when I tell you I see the exact timestamps where my EPCRs are being altered in the system... I am seeing things that are actually, physically there. The fact that other people around me claim they don't see it? That doesn't mean it's not happening. It just means they aren't paying attention, or... or worse, they're choosing to look the other way. Take my partner, for instance. He could absolutely see the camera tracking us if he just bothered to look up from scrolling on his phone for two seconds, but he doesn't. Or maybe he does see it and he's just too scared of the supervisors to say anything. I wouldn't blame him, honestly, knowing what they're capable of doing to a guy's career if he steps out of line. 

But no, I don't hear disembodied voices or see things that aren't there. Everything I'm dealing with is real, tangible, documented interference by the administration. And honestly, doc, you asking me that... it really makes me feel like you're just trying to find a way to write me off instead of actually listening to the very real, very serious situation I am trying to explain to you. I need you to focus on the facts of what they are doing to my reports, not on... on imaginary voices.
Do you ever realize that the bag-arranging and number-repeating might be excessive or unreasonable, even for a moment?

Excessive? Unreasonable? No, no, you're... you're looking at this exactly the way my lieutenant did, and it's just so incredibly frustrating because nobody is looking at the actual stakes here. That's actually the whole reason they forced me to come here, you know. That specific incident. 

I was down in the bay at the station. And I was moving the airway bags. The intubation kits, the pediatric roll-outs, the CPAP masks... I was moving them into this very specific pattern. A pattern that I just *knew* was right. It's hard to explain how I knew, but when you look at the spatial arrangement of the rig and the way the energy flows through the garage, there is a correct sequence for where those bags need to sit, and I was putting them exactly where they needed to be. And while I was doing it, I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. You have to repeat the numbers, you see, because the dispatch numbers are the variables, and speaking them out loud... it anchors the physical bags to the sequence. 

So I'm doing this, doing exactly what I have to do, and my lieutenant comes marching down into the bay. And he tells me to stop. He orders me to step away from the equipment. But I wouldn't do it. I couldn't do it. I flat out refused to step away, because... well, because I could feel it. I could feel this immense pressure building up in the air around me, and I knew, I knew with absolute certainty, that if I broke the sequence, if I stopped moving those bags and stopped repeating those numbers before the pattern was locked in, the whole bay would go bad. The entire ambulance bay. It would just... turn. Like milk going sour, but worse, like the whole structural integrity and the safety of the station would just collapse and go completely wrong. Everything would be ruined.

So how is that excessive? If you knew that stopping a sequence would cause a catastrophic failure in your workplace, would you just stop because your boss told you it looked weird? Of course not. You'd finish the pattern. You'd protect the bay. But he didn't see it that way. He just saw me moving the bags and talking out loud, decided it was 'unreasonable', pulled me off shift, and mandated I come see you. So no, I don't think it's excessive for even a second. I think it was absolutely, undeniably necessary.
Do you find these bag-arranging and number-repeating thoughts distressing or upsetting to you?

Distressing? No, why would they be distressing? It's... it's exactly the opposite, actually. Doing it is what keeps things right. The thoughts themselves, the numbers, the pattern with the bags... they aren't upsetting at all. They're clear. It's like... imagine you're driving the rig, right? You're looking through a dirty windshield for hours, you're driving into the sun, there's glare everywhere, you can barely see the lanes, and then suddenly you hit the wiper fluid and it just clears perfectly. That's what the sequence feels like. It's clarity. It's knowing exactly how the physical space of the bay needs to be anchored. 

What's distressing, what's actually upsetting, is people like my lieutenant not understanding it and getting in the way. I'm standing there, I've got the pediatric roll-out in my left hand, I'm calculating the spatial distance to the CPAP masks, I'm repeating the dispatch numbers—like, 4-1-niner-2-delta, whatever the exact variables were for that shift—and I'm building this... this necessary structure to keep the bay from going bad. And the whole time, I feel completely focused. I feel completely tuned in to the environment. There is absolutely no distress in the action itself. It's a responsibility. It's exactly like checking the main O2 tanks at the start of a shift. You don't get upset checking the oxygen, right? You do it because if you don't, the system fails. You do it because it's required. 

So no, the thoughts aren't upsetting in the slightest. The only upsetting part of that entire night was having a supervisor march down the stairs, completely oblivious to the energetic pressure building up in the room, yelling at me to stop. That was distressing. Because he was risking the entire structural integrity of the station just to assert his authority over me. If he had just let me finish the sequence with the airway bags, if he had just let me speak the numbers until the pattern was locked, everything would have been perfectly fine. But instead he interrupts a critical sequence, and now I'm sitting here, having to defend something that was completely necessary to someone who wasn't even there to feel the pressure in the room.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt persistently depressed or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Depressed? I don't... I don't know if 'depressed' is the word I'd use, because that implies I'm sitting around crying or feeling sad about things, and it's really not that. It's not sadness. But the interest part? The losing interest in things? Yeah. Yeah, I guess that's been happening for a while now. Definitely more than two weeks. 

Look, most days lately, I just sit in my apartment. I just sit there on the couch. And it's not like I'm doing anything productive or even relaxing, really. I'll just be sitting there, and I'll look over, and there's just this pile of trash in the corner. Just sitting there. And I see it, I know it needs to be bagged up and taken out to the bins out back, but I just... I don't do it. I can't even get myself to get up and grab a garbage bag. 

And my kitchen is the same way. I used to be really big on cooking. I'd do all this meal prep, you know? Because when you're working 12-hour shifts on the rig, if you don't prep your own meals, you end up eating gas station taquitos at three in the morning and it completely destroys your stomach. So I used to love cooking, I'd make these big batches of chicken and rice, really get into the whole process of it. But now? There's food still in the fridge right now. Good groceries I bought, just sitting in the crisper drawers, probably going bad as we speak because I just haven't cooked any of it. I haven't cooked like I used to in... I don't even know how long. 

And it's the same deal with the guys from the station. We used to have this pickup basketball game. Me and a couple of the other EMTs and a dispatcher, we'd hit the courts down at the rec center to get some cardio in and blow off steam after a bad rotation. But I haven't been calling the guys for basketball at all lately. My phone will be right there on the coffee table, and I could just send a text, just one quick text to see who's playing, but I don't. I just stare at it. It's like... it's like the starter motor in my brain is just completely burned out. I just can't get myself to care about the game, or the groceries, or the trash... I just can't get myself to start anything. So I just sit there. I don't know if you write that down as depression, doc, but... yeah, I'm just not doing much of anything these days.
When the bag-arranging or number-repeating starts, do you ever recognize that it might be irrational or coming from your own mind?

Irrational? Coming from my own mind? Doc, I feel like we're just going in circles here. I keep trying to explain the actual reality of the situation to you, and you keep trying to make it sound like it's just some... some daydream or a trick my brain is playing on me. 

Like I was just saying, the entire reason they sent me here, the whole reason I'm even sitting in this office talking to you right now, is because of what happened at the station. I kept moving those airway bags into a pattern that I absolutely, fundamentally knew was right. It wasn't a guess, and it wasn't something I just cooked up in my own head for fun. The space demanded it. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud because that is how you lock the physical items to the sequence. 

And when my lieutenant marched in and told me to stop... I wouldn't step away. I completely refused to step away from the rig, because it wasn't just an idea in my head. It was a physical reality. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. 

How can that just be in my mind? Think about it. If you're standing in a room and you suddenly smell smoke, you don't stop and ask yourself, 'Gee, is this fire just coming from my own mind? Is this irrational?' No! You react to the physical reality of the smoke. You pull the alarm. That's exactly what this is. The pattern with the airway bags, speaking the variables... it's a necessary response to a real, tangible pressure building up in the garage. If it was just in my head, I could just turn it off, right? I could have just said, 'Sure thing, Lieutenant, my mistake,' dropped the pediatric kit, and walked into the breakroom to grab a coffee. 

But I didn't do that. I couldn't do that, because the stakes were external. The structural safety of the station was literally at risk. So no, I don't ever sit there thinking it's irrational. I sit there realizing that I'm apparently the only person on shift actually paying attention to how the physical space is operating, and it's incredibly exhausting having to constantly defend that to people who just want to write it off as something broken in my brain.
Have the beliefs about the bags, numbers, cameras, and report changes only been present during this period of low mood and loss of interest?

Well, I mean... I don't know if I'd link them together like that, like one is causing the other or something. Because the sitting around my apartment, the trash piling up, not texting the guys for basketball... that's just been this gradual thing where my battery just completely ran out. But the other stuff? The really critical stuff? 

The camera and paperwork stuff, and the station behavior that got everyone so alarmed... that's been going on for about the last two months. A solid two months of it. 

And you really have to understand what those two months have actually been like for me. It's not just some fleeting thing. For two whole months, I've been having to constantly look over my shoulder and double-check my patient care reports because I know the variables are being changed after I file them. For two months, I've been walking into the ambulance bay and feeling that... that intense physical pressure, that energetic weight I was telling you about, and realizing that the cameras up in the corners aren't just passively recording, they're actively tied into the whole system. 

It started about eight weeks ago, just noticing a discrepancy here or feeling the air get heavy around the oxygen tanks there, but it's just built and built. And it is incredibly exhausting, doc. I mean, wouldn't you be exhausted? You try going sixty days straight where you're the only one on the entire roster who is actually maintaining the structural integrity of your workplace. You try being the only one who sees that the dispatch numbers and the airway bags have to be anchored just right to keep things from falling apart. 

And then, after two months of me quietly carrying that massive burden, two months of me keeping the station safe while everyone else is just blindly walking around drinking coffee... I finally have to take direct, visible action to secure the pediatric rollout on the rig, and suddenly *I'm* the problem. Suddenly everyone is alarmed and my lieutenant is yelling at me and sending me here. It's just... it's been two months of absolute, undeniable clarity about what's happening, and two months of nobody else bothering to open their eyes to see it. So yeah, two months for all of that. Whether that lines up with the basketball thing or not, I don't know, but that's the timeline.
During the past two months, have you had a period of feeling unusually high, energized, or euphoric?

High? Energized? Doc, I... I really don't think you're hearing me. I mean, we just went over this. If you were really listening to what I've been laying out for you about the last two months, you wouldn't even need to ask if I've been feeling euphoric. Euphoric? Like I'm on top of the world or bouncing off the walls? No. Absolutely not. Not even for a minute. 

I mean, just think about the actual logistics of it. I just told you I can't even get myself off the couch to throw away a single garbage bag. I can't even pick up my phone to send a five-word text to the guys about a pickup game. My battery is completely, fundamentally dead. There is zero energy in the tank. 

And then, when I am at work, doing these grueling 12-hour shifts on the rig, I'm carrying the weight of the entire station's physical reality on my shoulders. Do you have any idea how physically and mentally draining that is? To be the only one making sure the airway bags are aligned right and the dispatch numbers are locked in so the whole place doesn't just... go bad? There's no energy left for feeling high. There's no room for euphoria when you're the only one keeping the structural integrity intact for your crew. 

It's just a constant, grinding, bone-deep exhaustion. I go straight from my apartment, where I'm practically glued to the cushions, to the ambulance bay, where I have to expend every single ounce of focus I possess just to keep the variables from shifting. So no, I haven't felt energized at all. I haven't felt anything even remotely close to that. It's just been this heavy, heavy weight, every single day.
During the times you’ve felt down and unmotivated, were the beliefs about the cameras and report changes still there?

Well, yeah, of course they were. They never stopped. That’s what I’m trying to get you to understand about this whole situation. When I’m sitting on my couch, completely drained, unable to even gather the energy to take a single garbage bag to the dumpster... the reality of what's happening at the station doesn't just pause. 

While I'm stuck there feeling completely dead inside, I know exactly what's going on behind my back. I know for an absolute, undeniable fact that the injury review people—the ones who audit our calls and look for liabilities—and some of the supervisors at the station have been watching me. They use the security cameras in the bay and the supply rooms to monitor my every move. And it’s not just watching. They take what they see on those cameras, and then they go into the computer system after my shift and they actually change my triage notes. 

I’ll sit there in the rig, typing up a perfectly accurate patient care report, documenting the airway status, the vitals, exactly how the scene played out... and then later, I'll check, and the variables have been shifted. They alter my documentation specifically to make me look unsafe. To make it look like I'm making mistakes or putting patients at risk, which I would never do. I'm the only one keeping the station safe! 

And you know what the worst part is? The part that just completely drains whatever tiny bit of motivation I might have left? When I try to bring it up to them, when I point out that the triage notes have clearly been tampered with, they just look at me and say it’s just routine paperwork. They try to play it off like it's a standard audit update or some administrative correction. Routine paperwork! As if I don't know my own reports. As if I don't know exactly what I typed into the toughbook. 

So yeah, doc, when my battery is at zero and I can't even text my friends back, that is exactly what is hanging over my head. How are you supposed to feel motivated to do anything when you know the injury review board and your own supervisors are actively rewriting your reality to set you up? You can't. It never stops. Whether I'm paralyzed on the couch or standing in the garage, they're doing it.
Have the beliefs about the cameras and report changes ever happened when you were not feeling depressed or down?

I mean... I don't really know how to answer that, doc. Because, like I've been trying to explain, this whole situation—the cameras in the bay, the injury review people altering my paperwork, that total, absolute drain on my battery—it's all tied to right now. It's all been these last two months. 

Before that? I haven't noticed anything like that before. I mean, before this started, I wasn't feeling down at all. I was just living my life, you know? I was going to work, running my 12-hour shifts, hanging out with the guys, playing basketball... I was the EMT they relied on for the tough calls. And back then, I didn't have this... this crushing weight keeping me glued to the couch cushions. I wasn't depressed, or whatever word you want to use for it. 

And back then, the cameras in the bay were just cameras. The supervisors weren't actively coming after me. So, no, I haven't noticed the triage notes being changed when I felt normal, because when I felt normal, none of this was happening. The reality of them targeting me to make me look unsafe, and the reality of me having absolutely zero energy in the tank... they're just happening right now. At the exact same time. It's like, how could I even separate the two? I really don't know if the camera stuff could happen when I'm not feeling drained, because I haven't felt anything but completely drained since they started doing all this to me.
